title: Login route with JWT
idea: A login route checks an email and password against the stored hash. If they match, it signs a JWT and returns it as `{ token }`.
points: `bcrypt.compare` re-hashes the attempt with the salt stored in the hash.
The service returns `null` for an unknown email and for a wrong password.
`jwt.sign` stores `sub` (the user id as a string) and `email`, with `expiresIn: '1h'`.
The client sends the token back as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Lecture 12 checks it.

steps.caption: Ada sends her email and password to `POST /auth/login`.
Zod checks that the email is valid and a password is present.
The service looks up the email and finds Ada's row.
`bcrypt.compare` checks the password against the stored hash. It matches.
`jwt.sign` builds a token with `sub` and `email`, valid for one hour.
A second request has no password. It reaches Zod.
Zod rejects it, so the route sends `400` with the issues. The database is untouched.
A third request uses an email nobody registered. It passes Zod and reaches the lookup.
No row comes back. The route sends `401 Invalid email or password`.
A fourth request has Ada's email and the wrong password. It reaches `compare`.
`compare` fails. The client gets the same `401` and the same message, so it cannot tell the cases apart.

code.title: Login with a signed token
code.caption: The schema, service and controller are new. Everything under the setup comment lets this file run alone.

walk.text: Login needs a valid email and a non-empty password. Signup already enforced the length.
Find the user by email. No row means `null`.
`compare` checks the attempt against the stored hash. Return `id` and `email`, never the hash.
A bad body gets `400`. No user, or a wrong password, gets one `401`.
Sign `sub` and `email` with the secret. `expiresIn: '1h'` sets the expiry. Reply `{ token }`.
Setup: a demo secret, the `users` table, and Ada with a hashed password.
Log in and decode the token. Then try a wrong password, an unknown email and no password.

pitfalls: Use one message for both failures. Two messages tell attackers which emails have accounts.
Keep the password and `passwordHash` out of the claims. Anyone can decode a token.
Read `JWT_SECRET` from the environment. `demo-secret` is a demo value; never ship it.

quiz.why: A wrong password and a missing user both return `null`. The controller cannot tell them apart, so it sends the same `401`.

takeaway: Compare the password with the stored hash, then sign a token that expires.

starters: Can an attacker still tell the two failures apart by response time?
How long should a login token last?
What does the client do when the token expires?
